rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own two-season field monitoring (2018, 2019) with Sentek capacitance probes in commercial center-pivot potato fields in New Mexico, soil water balance ET estimates, and OpenET satellite ET retrievals.
rows.notes: The study reports no tuber yield data at all and no control (non-sensor) plots. Its own results concern soil water dynamics by depth, the effective rooting zone (upper 40 cm), and seasonal ET estimated by water balance (580 and 645 mm), FAO two-step method and OpenET. The passage's 6.6% yield increase, control plots, farmer-reported 15% water saving and time saving do not appear anywhere in the study; the only statement is an unsupported abstract sentence that probe-based scheduling improved irrigation water management. The claim therefore has no own evidence in this study.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own field monitoring with soil moisture probes across five (2018) and four (2019) commercial potato fields, with measured irrigation amounts and water-balance ET.
rows.notes: The study reports applied irrigation (seasonal average 777 <U+00B1> 36 mm) under sensor-based scheduling but has no comparison with a non-sensor or conventional scheduling treatment, so it cannot show water savings from sensors. There is no farmer survey, no reported 15% water reduction, and no assessment of time/effort for irrigation management. The abstract's statement that probe-based scheduling improved irrigation water use is an assertion not backed by any comparative result. Own results concern soil water profile dynamics, rooting depth and ET method comparison (water balance vs FAO Kc vs OpenET).

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a descriptive monitoring study of soil water and ET under sensor-scheduled sprinkler potato; it contains none of the quantitative yield, water-saving or farmer-reported figures attributed to it in the review passage, suggesting a citation error by the review.
